idiom_name: dirty set keyed by identity + write-behind queue + flush trigger
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: the change tracker keeps one entry per persisted identity holding the latest values plus enough original state to compute the delta; the flush trigger fires at the commit boundary, on a watermark, or on a timer; the flusher drains the queue, resolves it to one operation per identity, groups operations by target table, and executes the batch in one transaction. Nothing here is free: the developer supplies the accumulator, the coalescing rule, the boundary, and the failure policy. The classic structure is justified when write throughput or transaction economy dominates; otherwise immediate writes are simpler and honest about durability.
code_sketch:
stage(id, values):                  # producer: never writes
    dirty[id] = merge(dirty[id], values)
flush_trigger:                      # commit | watermark | timer
    batch = take(dirty)             # coalesced: one entry per id
    begin()
    for group in by_table(batch):
        write(group)                # ordered, one statement per id
    commit()
pitfalls: Coalescing without a durable buffer turns a crash into silent data loss.
A flush trigger that is not wired into shutdown and error paths leaves staged writes behind.

Wrong move: switch to FlushMode.MAL...mid-transaction -> JPQL, criteria, and native reads in the same session silently miss the staged rows and any forgotten flush persists nothing -> keep AUTO (it flushes at commit and before overlapping queries) and flush explicitly only where a query lacks synchronization.

Wrong move: flush the dirty set as delta statements (UPDATE t SET n = n + d) so the batch carries the change -> at-least-once replay double-applies the delta and an out-of-order batch corrupts the row -> flush the absolute final staged state as a version-guarded upsert so a replayed batch is idempotent.

Wrong move: enlarge the async queue and swallow failures (failSilently) so nothing blocks or errors -> under sustained pressure the queue fills and every writer blocks anyway, or errors vanish and the store silently diverges -> monitor queue depth, choose the block-or-drop overflow policy explicitly, and route failed writes to a durable retry path instead of the log.
